transcript.text: the door on our built in dishwasher just crashes down when you open it now, used to stay put. Hotpoint I think

That's almost always the **door balance springs**. There's one on each side at the bottom of the dishwasher, connected to the door hinge by a short cord or cable. When a spring snaps, or its cord breaks or slips off its pulley, nothing holds the door's weight, so it drops.

## Quick check
- Open the door partway and let go. If it falls hard to one side or feels lopsided, probably only one side has failed.
- Listen when opening. A twang or scraping noise often means a broken cord.
- On a built-in model the heavy kitchen-unit panel on the front adds weight, which wears the springs and cords out faster.

## Fixing it
1. **Turn off the power** at the isolator switch or plug, and shut off the water if you'll be moving the machine far.
2. **Remove the kickboard/plinth** under the dishwasher. On some models that's enough to see the springs.
3. If you can't reach them, **undo the screws holding the dishwasher to the worktop** (usually through brackets at the top front, sometimes through the sides into the cabinets) and slide it out a few inches. Mind the hoses.
4. **Look along the bottom sides** for:
   - a snapped spring
   - a spring hooked onto nothing
   - a broken or frayed cord or cable
   - a cord that's slipped off its small plastic pulley
5. **Replace both sides together**, even if only one has broken. The other is the same age and will go soon.

## Getting the right parts
- Find the **model number** on the sticker along the inner edge of the door (open it and look at the top or side rim). Hotpoint models usually start with letters like LTF, HIC, HIO or HIE.
- Search "**[model number] door spring kit**" or "door hinge cord kit". Kits often include springs, cords and pulleys and are usually cheap (roughly £10–25).
- Some kits come with springs in different strengths. Integrated models with heavy panels may need the stronger ones, or the tension adjusted using the holes the spring hooks into.

## When it's not the springs
If the springs and cords look fine, a **hinge** itself may be broken or bent. That's a bigger job but still fixable.

If you tell me the model number, I can help narrow down which kit you need.

Thanks. I heard a twang last week when it went. The sticker on the door edge is partly peeled but I can see it starts LTF. Can't pull the machine out though, it's screwed to the worktop and the plinth is tight.

The twang pretty much confirms it: a spring or its cord has snapped.

## Getting the full model number
The door sticker isn't the only place to find it:
- **Other stickers**: check the side edge of the inner door or the frame around the tub opening.
- **Paperwork**: the manual, receipt, or warranty card, if you have them.
- **Phone photo**: shining a torch at an angle can bring out faded print.
- Even partial digits help. "LTF" plus a few numbers is often enough to match a spring kit, since many LTF models share parts.

## Getting the plinth off
Integrated plinths usually just clip on:
- Pull firmly **straight out from the bottom edge**, ideally starting at one end. A flat scraper or putty knife slid underneath helps lever it without marking it.
- Some have **clips on the back that grip the cabinet legs**. Wiggle along the length as you pull.
- If it won't budge at all, look underneath with a torch for a screw or bracket.

Once it's off, you may be able to see the springs and replace them without moving the machine at all.

## Undoing the worktop screws
They're easier to find than they look:
1. Open the door fully.
2. Look at the **top edge of the dishwasher's front frame**, just under the worktop. There are usually two metal brackets with screws going up into the worktop.
3. Undo those. Sometimes there are also screws through the **sides of the frame** into the cabinets.
4. Lower the **front feet** a little (adjustable at the bottom front) so the top clears the worktop, then ease it forward a few inches.

If you can get the plinth off, have a look underneath and tell me what you see. I can talk you through it from there.
I managed to get a torch under the plinth and can see a loose spring hanging down on the right side. The left side seems to still have some tension. What should I do next?

That confirms the right-side spring assembly has failed. Here's what to do next.

## 1. Work out what broke
Shine the torch on the loose spring and check both ends:
- **Spring snapped**: a hook end is broken off, or the coil has split.
- **Cord or cable snapped**: the spring is intact but the cord hanging from it is frayed or cut.
- **Just came unhooked**: everything's intact but detached. You might be able to hook it back on, but it'll likely happen again if the parts are worn.

If you can, unhook the loose spring and take it out. It helps you match the replacement, and spring kits sometimes list the length.

## 2. Order a kit for both sides
- Search "**Hotpoint LTF door spring and cord kit**" plus any extra digits from the sticker.
- Compare the photos to your loose spring: length, hook style, and whether it uses a cord or a cable.
- Replace **both sides**. The left one has been carrying the whole door this past week and won't last much longer.

## 3. Fitting the new springs
Do this with the **door closed**, when the springs are least stretched.

1. Turn off the power at the isolator or plug.
2. Each assembly runs from a **fixed point near the back or bottom of the base**, through a **small pulley**, to the **door hinge arm** near the front.
3. Do one side at a time so you can copy the other side's layout.
4. Unhook the old spring and cord, thread the new cord the same way round the pulley, and hook it to the hinge.
5. Open and close the door a few times. It should stay put at about halfway and close smoothly.

## 4. Access
The hinge end of the cord is often up beside the tub, so you may not reach it through the plinth alone. If you can't reach it, you'll need the worktop screws out and the machine eased forward a few inches, as described earlier.

## Until it's fixed
Open the door gently with a hand underneath it. With only one spring left, it'll drop hard, which can damage the hinges.

If you send a description or photo of the broken end, I can help confirm which part failed.
